html:
The Maya built a civilisation of rival city-states in southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and western Honduras and El Salvador, lasting from before 1000 BCE until the Spanish took the last independent Maya kingdom in 1697. They were never one empire.

Their story falls into periods:

  • Preclassic (to about 250 CE): farming villages grew maize, beans, squash and chili peppers. The first cities appeared around 750 BCE, and writing by the 3rd century BCE.
  • Classic (about 250 to 900): the great age of cities such as Tikal, Calakmul, Copán and Palenque. Kings raised carved monuments dated in the Long Count calendar and fought constant wars. Distant Teotihuacan even meddled in Tikal's politics (see its intervention).
  • Collapse (about 800 to 900): the cities of the southern lowlands were abandoned, probably from a mix of drought, warfare and overuse of land. The north carried on.
  • Postclassic (900 to the 1500s): Chichén Itzá and later Mayapán led the northern Yucatán.

The Maya had the most developed writing in the Americas (see Maya script), and fine mathematics and astronomy, including a sign for zero. The Spanish conquest was slow because there was no single capital to seize. Nojpetén, on an island in a lake in Guatemala, held out until 1697.

The Maya did not vanish. More than six million people speak Mayan languages today, in much the same region.
